text: Build 3. New rule on top of the old one: if the skeptic can find it with a search, it's dead. Four pitches, and they all lean on the sky engine we built last time.
Mine: your birthday star. The star whose light left it the year you were born, so you're the same age as the light.
Dead. Starlust has a calculator for exactly that, and PBS has a table.
Mine: hear your birth sky. Every star above you that night becomes a note.
Dead. Stellart plays melodies from the stars' positions on any date you pick, and Stellar Symphony is open source.
Mine: your initials, spelled with real stars.
Dead. StarSpelled finds real stars that trace your letters. Someone showed it on Hacker News.
Mine: the stars under your feet, the ones on the other side of the planet right now.
Dead. SkySafari literally has a setting called Stars Beneath Your Feet. Four for four. Try harder.
Fine. GeoGuessr, but the sky. You get dropped under the real night sky over a mystery city on a mystery night. Guess where on Earth you are and what month it is.

Searched the web and GitHub for it. The names SkyGuessr and StarGuessr are taken, by a Minecraft map game, a flight-route puzzle and a star-spectrum quiz. The closest real thing, Stellar Guesser, quizzes you on star names and coordinates. Nothing I found shows you a sky and asks where on Earth and when. That doesn't prove nobody has, but it survives. And it passes the old test: people already play GeoGuessr with friends.
And it's fair. Sailors found their latitude from the height of the North Star for centuries. The sky really does tell you where and when.

Here's the plan. 1) Reuse the sky engine from build 2 2) Where the sun is, so every round is a real night 3) Mystery rounds: a city, a night, a time 4) Scoring: how far off, how many months off 5) A world map to click your guess on 6) The game page 7) A score line to paste to a friend One step at a time, a test with each, and the skeptic checks every one.

text: That red test is my fault: I guessed Boston-a-month-late would score over 4,000, and it scores 3,961. I committed before running the tests.

Doesn't matter now. CH read the pitch and said it's impossible for humans, and CH is right. Every city on the same latitude sees the same sky at the same local time, so nobody can guess longitude from stars. I checked whether it existed. I never checked whether a person could play it. That one's on me.
Build stopped after 4 of 7 steps. Third rule from now on: a normal person has to be able to actually do it.
Mine: the moon on every birthday of your life, in one row.
Dead. vorble/birthdaymoons on GitHub finds the full and new moons on your birthday.
Mine: you and someone you love, two birthdays, two cities. One map of the stars that were above you both.

Searched. Shops sell pairs of birth-sky maps side by side, like Under Lucky Stars. Nothing I found puts both skies on one map and finds the stars you share. A person can do it: type two birthdays. You'd send it to the person. It survives. And it reuses the sky engine, so it's cheap.

Here's the plan. 1) Reuse the sky engine from build 2 2) Which stars two skies share 3) One map with both skies: yours, theirs, and shared in gold 4) The page: two birthdays, two cities 5) A short link to send to the other person One step at a time, a test with each, and the skeptic checks every one.
